topic.subject: science
topic.title: Stars and the solar system
topic.scope: Moon phases, stars and constellations, planets, satellites, why the Moon shines, Pole Star

misconceptions.statement: The Moon produces its own light like a bulb.
misconceptions.why: The Moon appears very bright in the dark sky, leading students to think it is a source of light.
misconceptions.fix: The Moon is a non-luminous object that only reflects the sunlight falling on it.

probe.question: If the Sun were to suddenly disappear, would we still see a bright Moon at night?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because the Moon has its own light.

misconceptions.source_hint: HBCSE diagnostic studies on celestial objects

misconceptions.statement: Moon phases are caused by the Earth's shadow falling on the Moon.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse phases with lunar eclipses because both involve darkness on the Moon.
misconceptions.fix: Phases occur because we only see the part of the Moon's illuminated half that faces Earth as it orbits us.

probe.question: What causes the change in the shape of the Moon every night?
probe.wrong_answer: The Earth comes between the Sun and the Moon, casting a shadow.

misconceptions.root_belief: Shadows cause all darkness in space

misconceptions.statement: Stars go away or disappear during the daytime.
misconceptions.why: Stars are not visible during the day due to the Sun's glare, so students assume they are gone.
misconceptions.fix: Stars are always in the sky, but they are hidden during the day by the bright light of the Sun.

probe.question: Where do the stars go when the Sun rises?
probe.wrong_answer: They move to the other side of the Earth or disappear.

misconceptions.root_belief: What you cannot see does not exist
misconceptions.source_hint: Rosalind Driver's Children's Ideas in Science

misconceptions.statement: The Pole Star is the brightest star in the night sky.
misconceptions.why: Because the Pole Star is famous and important for navigation, students assume it must be the brightest.
misconceptions.fix: The Pole Star is only of average brightness; Sirius is actually the brightest star in the night sky.

probe.question: How can you identify the Pole Star in the sky?
probe.wrong_answer: By looking for the single brightest point of light in the sky.

misconceptions.statement: Stars actually move across the sky from East to West.
misconceptions.why: We see stars rising in the East and setting in the West, just like the Sun.
misconceptions.fix: Stars appear to move because the Earth is rotating on its axis from West to East.

probe.question: Why do stars change their position in the sky during the night?
probe.wrong_answer: Because stars are revolving around the Earth.

misconceptions.statement: The Sun is not a star because it looks different and is much larger.
misconceptions.why: The Sun appears as a huge, hot disc while stars appear as tiny twinkling dots.
misconceptions.fix: The Sun is a medium-sized star that only looks large because it is much closer to Earth than other stars.

probe.question: Is the Sun a star?
probe.wrong_answer: No, the Sun is a sun and stars are those tiny things at night.

misconceptions.statement: Shooting stars are actual stars falling from the sky.
misconceptions.why: The term 'shooting star' suggests a star is moving or falling.
misconceptions.fix: Shooting stars are actually meteors—small pieces of rock entering Earth's atmosphere and burning up.

probe.question: What is a shooting star made of?
probe.wrong_answer: It is a star that has lost its balance and fallen.

misconceptions.statement: Stars in a constellation are all at the same distance from Earth.
misconceptions.why: They appear to be on a flat 2D plane (the sky) forming a pattern.
misconceptions.fix: Stars in a constellation are at vastly different distances from us; they only look close together from our perspective.

probe.question: Are the stars in the Big Dipper close to each other in space?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, they are a group located in the same spot in the universe.

misconceptions.statement: Planets twinkle just like stars do.
misconceptions.why: Planets look like bright dots in the sky, so students group them with stars.
misconceptions.fix: Planets do not twinkle because they are much closer and appear as tiny discs rather than point sources of light.

probe.question: How can you tell a planet apart from a star in the night sky?
probe.wrong_answer: You can't, because both of them twinkle at night.

misconceptions.root_belief: Distant lights are all the same

misconceptions.statement: Earth is the only planet that has a moon.
misconceptions.why: Students often refer to Earth's satellite as 'The Moon' and don't realize other planets have them too.
misconceptions.fix: Many planets in our solar system, like Jupiter and Saturn, have many natural satellites (moons).

probe.question: Do other planets have moons?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only Earth has a moon to give it light at night.

misconceptions.statement: The Moon changes shape because clouds cover parts of it.
misconceptions.why: Clouds often block the moon, and students associate covering an object with changing its visible shape.
misconceptions.fix: Moon phases are independent of weather; they are caused by the Moon's position relative to the Sun and Earth.

probe.question: If there were no clouds for a whole month, would the Moon still change shape?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it would stay a full circle the whole time.

misconceptions.root_belief: Visible changes are due to local obstructions
misconceptions.source_hint: Rosalind Driver's Children's Ideas in Science

misconceptions.statement: Stars are smaller than the Sun and the Moon.
misconceptions.why: Stars appear as tiny specks, while the Sun and Moon appear much larger in the sky.
misconceptions.fix: Most stars are actually much larger than the Sun and millions of times larger than the Moon.

probe.question: Which is actually larger: the Sun or the stars we see at night?
probe.wrong_answer: The Sun is much larger than those tiny stars.

misconceptions.statement: Planets move in perfect circles around the Sun.
misconceptions.why: Simplified diagrams in textbooks often show orbits as perfect circles.
misconceptions.fix: Planetary orbits are actually elliptical (oval-shaped), not perfect circles.

probe.question: What is the shape of the path a planet takes around the Sun?
